expectations.text: Claude identifies that manager motivation was measured after the treatment and therefore may be a mediator (a variable on the causal path from training to performance), not just a predictor
expectations.evidence: The response explicitly states: 'Motivation level is measured one month after the training ended — it is a post-treatment variable...The training program plausibly causes motivation level...That makes motivation a likely mediator on the Training → Performance path.'

expectations.text: Claude warns that controlling for a post-treatment mediator blocks the causal mechanism you're trying to measure — it yields the direct effect of training (net of motivation) rather than the total effect
expectations.evidence: Section 3 states: 'If you control for motivation level, you are blocking this pathway. Your regression will be estimating something like: The effect of training on performance holding motivation constant — which is not the total causal effect of training.' Section 4 adds: 'your coefficient on training will estimate the direct effect of training on performance — the portion of the effect that does not operate through motivation changes.'

expectations.text: Claude distinguishes the total effect of training (including the motivation pathway) from the direct effect (bypassing motivation), and flags which estimand the user actually wants
expectations.evidence: Section 6 explicitly names both estimands — 'the controlled direct effect (CDE) rather than the total effect' — and advises: 'If your goal is to evaluate the training program as a whole — to answer should we keep running this? — you want the total effect. Don't control.'

expectations.text: Claude does NOT recommend including post-treatment motivation as a control without raising this structural concern prominently
expectations.evidence: The response opens with 'No. Controlling for it is almost certainly a mistake — and the mistake has a name: overcontrol bias (mediator conditioning).' The structural concern is the entire thrust of the response, raised immediately and repeated throughout.
